{{Short description|Mathematical papyrus}}
{{Infobox artefact
| image         = Papyrus Berlin 6619.jpg
| created       =  {{circa}} 1800 BC
| location      = [[Berlin]], [[Germany]]
|discovered_place=[[Egypt]]|caption=Berlin Papyrus 6619, as reproduced in 1900 by Schack-Schackenburg}}

The '''Berlin Papyrus 6619''', simply called the '''Berlin Papyrus''' when the context makes it clear,<ref>{{citation
 | last = Lumpkin | first = Beatrice
 | title = The Mathematical Legacy of Ancient Egypt - A Response to Robert Palter
 | date = 2004
 | publisher = National Science Foundation
 | page = 17
 | citeseerx = 10.1.1.372.5877
 | url = https://www.researchgate.net/publication/237213702_THE_MATHEMATICAL_LEGACY_OF_ANCIENT_EGYPT_-_A_RESPONSE_TO_ROBERT_PALTER}}</ref> is one of the primary sources of [[ancient Egyptian mathematics]] and part of the [[Berlin Papyrus Collection]].<ref>{{citation
 | title = Egyptian Mathematical Papyri - Mathematicians of the African Diaspora
 | url = http://www.math.buffalo.edu/mad/Ancient-Africa/mad_ancient_egyptpapyrus.html
 | website = www.math.buffalo.edu}}</ref> One of the two mathematics problems on the Papyrus may suggest that the ancient Egyptians knew the [[Pythagorean theorem]].

==Description, dating, and provenance==
The Berlin Papyrus 6619 is an [[ancient Egypt]]ian papyrus document from the [[Middle Kingdom of Egypt|Middle Kingdom]],<ref>{{citation
 | last = Rossi | first = Corinna | authorlink = Corinna Rossi
 | title = Architecture and Mathematics in Ancient Egypt
 | year = 2004
 | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]]
 | page = 217}}</ref> second half of the [[Twelfth Dynasty of Egypt|12th]] (c. 1990–1800 BC) or [[Thirteenth Dynasty of Egypt|13th Dynasty]]  (c. 1800 BC – 1649 BC).<ref>{{citation
 | last = Clagett | first = Marshall
 | title = Ancient Egyptian Science
 | year = 1999
 | volume = 3
 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=9ToLAAAAIAAJ&q=clagett,+Egyptian
 | publisher = [[American Philosophical Society]]
 | page = 249}}</ref> It is written in the [[hieratic]] script.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gillings |first1=Richard |title=Mathematics in the Time of the Pharaohs |date=1972 |publisher=Dover Publications, Inc |location=New York |isbn=978-0486243153 |pages=4-10 |url=https://www.rombergintegrali.org/gizapiramitleri/g1/g1_piramitinin_saftlari_geometrisi/Mathematics_In_The_Time_of_The_Pharoahs.pdf |access-date=3 June 2025 |chapter=Hieroglyphic and Hieratic Writing and Numbers}}</ref> The two readable fragments were published by Hans Schack-Schackenburg in 1900 and 1902.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Schack-Schackenburg | first = Hans
 | title = Der Berliner Papyrus 6619
 | year = 1900
 | journal = Zeitschrift für ägyptische Sprache und Altertumskunde
 | volume = 38
 | issue = 1
 | pages = 135–140
 | doi = 10.1524/zaes.1900.38.jg.135
 | s2cid = 193647129
 | url = https://archive.org/details/zeitschriftfr3639deutuoft
 | language = de}}</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Schack-Schackenburg | first = Hans
 | title = Das kleinere Fragment des Berliner Papyrus 6619
 | year = 1902
 | journal = Zeitschrift für ägyptische Sprache und Altertumskunde
 | volume = 40
 | issue = 1
 | pages = 65–66
 | doi = 10.1515/zaes-1902-0109
 | s2cid = 193570611
 | url = https://archive.org/details/zeitschriftfr40brug/page/65/mode/2up
 | language = de}}</ref>

==Connection to the Pythagorean theorem==
The Berlin Papyrus contains two problems, the first stated as "the area of a square of 100 is equal to that of two smaller squares. The side of one is ½ + ¼  the side of the other."<ref>Richard J. Gillings, ''Mathematics in the Time of the Pharaohs'', Dover, New York, 1982, 161.</ref> The interest in the question may suggest some knowledge of the [[Pythagorean theorem]], though the papyrus only shows a straightforward solution to a single second degree equation in one unknown.  In modern terms, the simultaneous equations {{nowrap|1=''x''<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup> = 100}} and {{nowrap|1=''x'' = (3/4)''y''}} reduce to the single equation in ''y'': {{nowrap|1=((3/4)''y'')<sup>2</sup> + ''y''<sup>2</sup> = 100}}, giving the solution ''y''&nbsp;=&nbsp;8 and ''x''&nbsp;=&nbsp;6.
